source: The slope of an x–t graph is the velocity.
Students read a high point on the graph as a high speed, mixing up the value with the slope.

A position-time ($x$–$t$) graph plots where an object is at each moment. Its most useful feature is its slope, which you can find with The Slope Formula. Over any straight piece, rise over run is $\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$, which is exactly the Average Velocity.
The slope of an $x$–$t$ graph is the velocity. Steeper means faster; upward slope means moving in the $+x$ direction; downward slope means $-x$; flat means standing still.

The rise of the graph is a change in position, $\Delta x$, and the run is a change in time, $\Delta t$. Dividing gives $\Delta x / \Delta t$, the definition of velocity. The height of the graph only tells you where the object is, not how fast it moves.
A walk in four pieces: forward, a stop, a fast stretch forward, then a long walk back.
On the graph above, find the velocity from $t = 5\ \text{s}$ to $t = 8\ \text{s}$.
On the same graph, when is the walker fastest?
Speed is the size of the slope, so the biggest is $4\ \text{m/s}$, from $4$ to $5\ \text{s}$.

Reading a high point on the graph as high speed. The top of the graph above ($x = 9\ \text{m}$ at $t = 5\ \text{s}$) is where the walker is farthest away, not where they move fastest; at the highest point of a curved graph, the object is momentarily stopped. Check: always ask "how steep?", never "how high?", when you want velocity.
